When AuthType is configured as NONE, requests can be accepted without AWS IAM authentication, potentially exposing the function to unauthenticated internet access if the associated resource policy permits public invocation. Publicly accessible Lambda Function URLs can increase the attack surface and may be abused for unauthorized access, denial-of-service activity, data exfiltration, command-and-control infrastructure, or other malicious purposes. Configuring Lambda Function URLs to use AWS_IAM ensures that requests are authenticated and authorized through AWS Identity and Access Management before the function is invoked.

attributes.RationaleStatement: Lambda Function URLs configured with AuthType = NONE create internet-reachable HTTPS endpoints that do not require AWS IAM authentication. Such endpoints may be unintentionally exposed, difficult to inventory, and susceptible to misuse. Requiring AWS_IAM authentication enforces identity-based access control, supports the principle of least privilege, and reduces the likelihood of unauthorized invocation or abuse of Lambda-hosted services.
attributes.ImpactStatement: Applications intentionally designed for public anonymous access may require architectural changes. Such workloads should instead be fronted by managed services such as API Gateway, CloudFront, or other approved ingress mechanisms that provide appropriate authentication, authorization, monitoring, and abuse protection controls.
attributes.RemediationProcedure: Update the Lambda Function URL configuration: aws lambda update-function-url-config --function-name <function-name> --auth-type AWS_IAM
attributes.AuditProcedure: Identify Lambda Function URLs where: aws lambda list-function-url-configs Review the value of: "AuthType": "NONE" Any Lambda Function URL configured with AuthType other than AWS_IAM should be considered a finding.
attributes.DefaultValue: No default value. The authentication type must be explicitly configured when creating a Lambda Function URL.

requirements.name: Ensure Lambda functions accessing private resources or sensitive data are deployed within a customer managed VPC
requirements.description: By default, Lambda functions run in an AWS managed VPC with unrestricted outbound internet access. Functions that access private resources, such as RDS or internal APIs or that process sensitive data such as PII, should instead be deployed within a customer managed VPC to enforce network boundary controls through security groups and network ACLs.

attributes.RationaleStatement: Without VPC configuration, Lambda functions have unrestricted outbound access, meaning sensitive data could be exfiltrated with no network level controls in place to detect or stop it. Security groups, network ACLs, and standard network monitoring tools cannot be applied to functions outside a VPC. This is required under frameworks such as FedRAMP and is auditable today using the AWS Config managed rule lambda inside vpc.
attributes.ImpactStatement: Deploying functions within a VPC may increase cold start latency and requires a NAT gateway for outbound internet access, along with additional IAM permissions for network interface management (may have additional costs). These tradeoffs are well documented by AWS and proportionate for functions handling sensitive data.
attributes.RemediationProcedure: From the Console 1. Navigate to the non compliant function, open Configuration, then VPC, then Edit 2. Select the target VPC and at least two private subnets across different Availability Zones 3. Select or create security groups enforcing least privilege for inbound and outbound traffic 4. Save the configuration
attributes.AuditProcedure: From the Console 1. Navigate to AWS Lambda 2. For each function, open Configuration, then VPC 3. Confirm a customer managed VPC, subnets, and security groups are configured 4. Functions showing No VPC that access private resources or sensitive data are non compliant 5. Repeat for each function in the current region, then repeat for all other regions
attributes.AdditionalInformation: This control is most relevant in regulated industries such as financial services, healthcare and government, where Lambda functions frequently process PII or other sensitive data. It serves as the prerequisite to FSBP Lambda.5, which assumes VPC connectivity already exists. For stronger enforcement, Lambda specific IAM condition keys, lambda VpcIds, lambda SubnetIds and lambda SecurityGroupIds, can require VPC deployment at the IAM policy level. This proposal is based on direct implementation experience in a regulated financial services environment.
attributes.DefaultValue: By default, Lambda functions are not deployed within VPC and have unrestricted outbound internet access.

requirements.name: Ensure communications between your applications and clients is encrypted.
requirements.description: SimSpace Weaver doesn't manage communications between your apps and the clients.

attributes.RationaleStatement: Be sure to implement some form of authentication and encryption for all client sessions while using SimSpace Weaver.
attributes.RemediationProcedure: Confirm that the communication you have configured between you application and clients that run inside of SimSpace Weaver are encrypted.
attributes.AuditProcedure: There is no setting for encryption setup for your clients and applications within SimSpace Weaver service. For this audit you have to confirm that the communication is configured in the app and the client with encryption to protect that traffic.

requirements.name: Ensure Image Builder distribution configurations do not publicly share AMIs
requirements.description: EC2 Image Builder pipelines reference a distribution configuration that controls how the AMI produced by each pipeline run is shared. The distribution config's AmiDistributionConfiguration.LaunchPermission field can grant public access ({"UserGroups":["all"]}) so that every AMI built by the pipeline is published publicly on creation. This control audits Image Builder distribution configurations directly to catch misconfigured pipelines before they produce public AMIs on their next run.

attributes.RationaleStatement: AMIs contain the full filesystem of a configured instance, including pre-installed applications, configuration files, internal CA certificates, agent configurations, and potentially residual credentials. A publicly shared AMI allows any AWS account to launch an instance from it and inspect all contents.
attributes.ImpactStatement: Organizations that intentionally publish AMIs (community AMIs, AWS Marketplace offerings, open-source projects) and use Image Builder pipelines to do so must keep their public-distribution pipelines in dedicated accounts with this control disabled, while applying it to all production / internal accounts.
attributes.RemediationProcedure: 1. For each distribution configuration that Failed the audit, retrieve its current distributions block and remove the userGroups: ["all"] entry from each region's amiDistributionConfiguration.launchPermission. The remediation requires a full updated distribution config to be sent — the AWS API doesn't support patching individual fields: # Retrieve current config aws imagebuilder get-distribution-configuration --distribution-configuration- arn <arn> \ --region $AWS_REGION --query 'distributionConfiguration' > /tmp/dist- config.json # Edit /tmp/dist-config.json: in each distributions[].amiDistributionConfiguration.launchPermission, # remove the "userGroups": ["all"] entry. To restrict to specific accounts, replace with: # "userIds": ["<account-id-1>", "<account-id-2>"] # To make AMIs private to the source account only, remove the launchPermission key entirely. # Apply the updated config aws imagebuilder update-distribution-configuration --distribution- configuration-arn <arn> \ --region $AWS_REGION --distributions file:///tmp/dist-config.json 2. Verify by repeating audit step 2 on the distribution configuration. 3. Trigger a test run of any affected pipeline and verify the resulting AMI is not public: aws ec2 describe-images --owners self --filters Name=is-public,Values=true -- region $AWS_REGION \ --query 'Images[?starts_with(Name, `<image-builder- prefix>`)].[ImageId,Name,Public]' --output table
attributes.AuditProcedure: 1. List all Image Builder distribution configurations in the region: aws imagebuilder list-distribution-configurations --region $AWS_REGION \ --query 'distributionConfigurationSummaryList[].[name,arn]' --output table 2. For each distribution configuration returned above, inspect its AMI distribution settings to check whether any region grants public launch permissions: aws imagebuilder get-distribution-configuration --distribution-configuration- arn <arn> \ --region $AWS_REGION \ --query 'distributionConfiguration.distributions[].{Region:region,LaunchPermission:am iDistributionConfiguration.launchPermission}' \ --output json • The distribution configuration Fails if any region's launchPermission includes "userGroups": ["all"]. This indicates that AMIs produced by any pipeline using this distribution config will be publicly accessible. 3. For each distribution configuration that Failed the audit, identify the Image Builder pipelines that reference it (so you understand the blast radius): aws imagebuilder list-image-pipelines --region $AWS_REGION \ --filters name=distributionConfigurationArn,values=<arn> \ --query 'imagePipelineList[].[name,arn,status]' --output table

requirements.name: Ensure Image Builder pipelines do not disable the built-in security cleanup script
requirements.description: Before producing the final AMI snapshot, EC2 Image Builder runs a built-in security cleanup script on the build instance that securely removes cloud-init artifacts, SSH host keys and authorized_keys, instance log files, package manager logs, Task Orchestrator/Executor (TOE) working files, and SSM agent logs. This cleanup is enabled by default and runs automatically. However, AWS allows the cleanup to be partially or wholly disabled in two ways: (1) the recipe's components can create skip_cleanup_* flag files that suppress individual sections of the cleanup, or (2) the recipe can specify additionalInstanceConfiguration.userDataOverride, which disables the entire cleanup script unless that user data explicitly creates the perform_cleanup flag file.

attributes.RationaleStatement: The built-in cleanup exists to prevent residual sensitive artifacts — SSH host keys, authorized_keys containing operator public keys, installation logs that may contain tokens, cloud-init data, and SSM session logs — from persisting into the final AMI. When an instance is launched from an AMI that retained these artifacts, anyone with access to that instance (or to the AMI itself, if shared cross-account or made public) can extract them. Reusing baked-in SSH host keys across many launched instances also breaks SSH host-key trust models and enables impersonation. Bypassing the cleanup is rarely necessary; teams sometimes do it inadvertently when they supply a userDataOverride for build-time provisioning without realizing it disables cleanup, or when they add skip_cleanup_* files for debugging and forget to remove them.
attributes.ImpactStatement: Organizations with a legitimate need to preserve specific artifacts on the AMI (e.g., a baseline log file required by an internal compliance tool) must instead capture those artifacts out-of-band before the cleanup phase rather than skipping cleanup. Recipes that need a userDataOverride must include a step that creates the /var/lib/amazon/toe/perform_cleanup flag file so that the cleanup script still runs.
attributes.RemediationProcedure: 1. For components that Failed — remove the action that creates the skip_cleanup_* file from the component's data and publish a new component version, then update affected recipes to reference the new component version: aws imagebuilder create-component --name <component-name> --region $AWS_REGION \ --semantic-version <next-version> --platform Linux \ --data file://component-fixed.yaml 2. For recipes that Failed — image recipes are immutable, so create a new recipe version whose userDataOverride adds the perform_cleanup flag file before any other commands. • Publish the new recipe version with the corrected override: aws imagebuilder create-image-recipe --name <recipe-name> --region $AWS_REGION \ --semantic-version <next-version> --parent-image <parent-image> \ --components '[{"componentArn": "<component-arn>"}]' \ --additional-instance-configuration "userDataOverride=$(base64 -w0 user- data-fixed.sh)" • Update any pipelines using the old recipe to reference the new version. 18 Elastic Container Registry (ECR) Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR) is a fully-managed container image registry service that makes it easy to store, manage, share, and deploy container images and OCI (Open Container Initiative) artifacts without operating your own registry infrastructure. ECR integrates natively with AWS compute services that consume container images — Amazon ECS, Amazon EKS, AWS Fargate, and AWS Lambda — and supports private and public repositories, image scanning, lifecycle policies, cross- region and cross-account replication, immutable image tags, and pull-through caching from upstream registries.
attributes.AuditProcedure: The cleanup can be bypassed in two ways: (a) a recipe's additionalInstanceConfiguration.userDataOverride is set without re-enabling cleanup, or (b) a custom component creates a skip_cleanup_* flag file. 1. Identify any image recipes that have a userDataOverride configured: aws imagebuilder list-image-recipes --region $AWS_REGION \ --query 'imageRecipeSummaryList[].arn' --output text \ | xargs -n1 -I {} aws imagebuilder get-image-recipe --image-recipe-arn {} - -region $AWS_REGION \ --query 'imageRecipe.[arn, additionalInstanceConfiguration.userDataOverride]' --output table • For any recipe where the second column is not empty, base64-decode the override and review the script. The recipe Fails unless the script either (i) creates the file /var/lib/amazon/toe/perform_cleanup (which re-enables the built-in cleanup), or (ii) implements an equivalent organizational cleanup process to purge build artifacts, logs, and temporary credentials before AMI finalization. 2. Identify any custom components in use: aws imagebuilder list-components --owner Self --region $AWS_REGION \ --query 'componentVersionList[].arn' --output text \ | xargs -n1 -I {} aws imagebuilder get-component --component-build-version- arn {} --region $AWS_REGION \ --query 'component.[arn, data]' --output text • For each component, review the data field. The component Fails if it creates any skip_cleanup_* flag file (e.g., skip_cleanup_ssh_files, skip_cleanup_instance_log_files, skip_cleanup_toe_files) without a documented and approved exception. If neither step surfaces a recipe or component that bypasses cleanup, the account Passes for this region.

requirements.name: Ensure ECR repositories have image scanning enabled
requirements.description: Amazon ECR supports image scanning to identify known software vulnerabilities (CVEs) in container images. Two scan types are available: Basic scanning (Clair-based, free) provides OS package vulnerability detection, while Enhanced scanning (powered by Amazon Inspector) provides continuous monitoring of both OS packages and programming language libraries. Scan-on-push ensures every image is assessed before deployment.

attributes.RationaleStatement: Container images may contain base OS layers or application dependencies with known critical vulnerabilities. Without scanning, vulnerable images are deployed to production where they can be exploited by attackers. Image scanning provides visibility into known vulnerabilities before deployment and enables enforcement of vulnerability thresholds in CI/CD pipelines.
attributes.ImpactStatement: Enhanced scanning incurs Amazon Inspector costs per image assessed. Basic scanning is free but limited to OS packages. Enabling scan-on-push adds seconds to the image push workflow.
attributes.RemediationProcedure: Before remediating, teams should determine the appropriate scanning level for their workload: • Basic scanning — Free, Clair-based, scans OS packages only. Suitable for teams with cost sensitivity or where container images are thin OS layers only. • Enhanced scanning — Amazon Inspector-powered, scans OS packages plus programming language libraries, supports continuous rescanning. Suitable for teams deploying application code in containers where library CVEs are a concern. Incurs Amazon Inspector per-image assessment charges. Apply the remediation for whichever level you select. Option A — Enable Enhanced scanning (recommended for application workloads): aws ecr put-registry-scanning-configuration --region $AWS_REGION \ --scan-type ENHANCED \ --rules '[{"scanFrequency":"CONTINUOUS_SCAN","repositoryFilters":[{"filter":"*","filt erType":"WILDCARD"}]}]' • The put-registry-scanning-configuration call auto-enables Amazon Inspector for ECR. Valid scan frequencies under Enhanced scanning are SCAN_ON_PUSH (scan only when images are pushed) or CONTINUOUS_SCAN (push + ongoing rescans as new CVEs are disclosed — recommended). Option B — Enable Basic scanning per repository: For each repository that Failed the audit, enable scan-on-push: aws ecr put-image-scanning-configuration --region $AWS_REGION \ --repository-name <repo-name> \ --image-scanning-configuration scanOnPush=true
attributes.AuditProcedure: The ECR registry passes the audit procedure if either Basic or Enhanced scanning is enabled and covers all repositories. Enhanced (Amazon Inspector) is the stronger option as it scans both OS packages and programming language libraries; Basic (Clair- based) scans OS packages only. 1. Check the registry-level scanning configuration: aws ecr get-registry-scanning-configuration --region $AWS_REGION \ --query 'scanningConfiguration.{ScanType:scanType,Rules:rules}' --output json • If ScanType is ENHANCED with a rule covering all repositories ("filter":"*"), the registry Passes — skip the remaining steps. 2. If ScanType is BASIC, list all repositories in the region: aws ecr describe-repositories --region $AWS_REGION \ --query 'repositories[].repositoryName' --output table 3. For each repository returned above, check its scan-on-push setting: aws ecr describe-repositories --repository-names <repo-name> --region $AWS_REGION \ --query 'repositories[].imageScanningConfiguration.scanOnPush' --output text • Under BASIC scan mode, the repository Fails if the returned value is False.

requirements.name: Ensure ECR repositories have lifecycle policies configured
requirements.description: ECR lifecycle policies automatically expire old or untagged images based on age or count rules. Without lifecycle policies, repositories accumulate unlimited image versions over time, including untagged intermediate builds, old releases with known vulnerabilities, and images containing previously hardcoded secrets that have since been rotated.

attributes.RationaleStatement: Stale images present security risk in two ways: they can be accidentally deployed (reintroducing patched vulnerabilities), and they preserve a historical record of application security weaknesses accessible to anyone with repository read access. Lifecycle policies ensure repositories retain only recent, relevant images and automatically remove images that should no longer be available.
attributes.ImpactStatement: Lifecycle policies permanently delete images matching the expiration rules. Teams must ensure retention periods are sufficient for rollback requirements. Images needed for long-term archival should be stored separately.
attributes.RemediationProcedure: For each repository that Failed the audit, apply a lifecycle policy. The example below expires untagged images after 14 days and keeps only the last 30 tagged versions: aws ecr put-lifecycle-policy --repository-name <repo-name> --region $AWS_REGION \ --lifecycle-policy-text '{ "rules": [ { "rulePriority": 1, "description": "Expire untagged images after 14 days", "selection": { "tagStatus": "untagged", "countType": "sinceImagePushed", "countUnit": "days", "countNumber": 14 }, "action": {"type": "expire"} }, { "rulePriority": 2, "description": "Keep only last 30 tagged images", "selection": { "tagStatus": "tagged", "tagPrefixList": ["v"], "countType": "imageCountMoreThan", "countNumber": 30 }, "action": {"type": "expire"} } ] }'
attributes.AuditProcedure: 1. List all ECR repositories in the region: aws ecr describe-repositories --region $AWS_REGION \ --query 'repositories[].repositoryName' --output table 2. For each of the repositories returned above, check whether it has a lifecycle policy: aws ecr get-lifecycle-policy --repository-name <repo-name> --region $AWS_REGION • The repository Fails if the command returns LifecyclePolicyNotFoundException.

requirements.name: Ensure ECR repositories use immutable image tags
requirements.description: ECR repositories can be configured with either MUTABLE (default) or IMMUTABLE image tag mutability. When set to MUTABLE, an image tag can be overwritten by pushing a new image with the same tag. When set to IMMUTABLE, once a tag is assigned to an image, it cannot be reassigned to a different image.

attributes.RationaleStatement: Mutable image tags allow an attacker who gains push access to a repository (via compromised CI/CD credentials or overly permissive repository policies) to replace a legitimate image with a malicious one using the same tag (e.g., "latest", "v2.1.0"). When services pull the image by tag, they deploy the attacker's payload. Immutable tags ensure that a tagged image cannot be replaced, providing supply chain integrity guarantees.
attributes.ImpactStatement: CI/CD pipelines using overwrite-based tag strategies (e.g., always pushing to "latest") must be updated to use unique tags per build (commit SHA, build number, or semantic version). Rolling deployment strategies that rely on tag updates must use new tags instead.
attributes.RemediationProcedure: For each repository that Failed the audit, set image tag immutability: aws ecr put-image-tag-mutability --repository-name <repo-name> --region $AWS_REGION \ --image-tag-mutability IMMUTABLE
attributes.AuditProcedure: 1. List all ECR repositories in the region: aws ecr describe-repositories --region $AWS_REGION \ --query 'repositories[].repositoryName' --output table 2. For each repository returned above, check its image tag mutability setting: aws ecr describe-repositories --repository-names <repo-name> --region $AWS_REGION \ --query 'repositories[].imageTagMutability' --output text • The repository Fails if the returned value is MUTABLE. The Passing value is IMMUTABLE.

requirements.name: Ensure private ECR repositories do not allow public access via resource policies
requirements.description: Amazon ECR private repositories support resource-based IAM policies that grant other principals permission to pull, push, or describe images. A repository policy that grants ECR actions to Principal: "*" or AWS: "*" without a restrictive Condition makes the repository's images effectively public — any AWS account, and in some cases any unauthenticated caller, can read or modify them. This recommendation requires that no private ECR repository have a resource-based policy that grants ECR read or write actions to all principals without a Condition that limits access to specific accounts or organizations.

attributes.RationaleStatement: Container image layers in private repositories often contain proprietary application code, internal API endpoint configurations, embedded certificates, baked-in third-party credentials, and infrastructure details that can be used to identify application vulnerabilities. An overly permissive repository policy bypasses the implicit account boundary that private repositories provide and exposes these contents to anyone who can reach the ECR API.
attributes.ImpactStatement: Repositories that legitimately need to be shared with external accounts (e.g., partner organizations consuming a release feed) must restrict the principal explicitly to those account IDs or organization ID rather than grabting the blanket allow all.
attributes.RemediationProcedure: 1. For each repository that Failed the audit, retrieve the current policy and edit the offending statement so the principal is restricted to specific accounts (or removed if no cross-account access is needed): # Retrieve current policy aws ecr get-repository-policy --repository-name <repo-name> --region $AWS_REGION \ --query 'policyText' --output text > /tmp/repo-policy.json Edit '/tmp/repo-policy.json'. Replace "Principal": "*" (or "Principal": {"AWS": "*"}) with one of the following, depending on the intent: • No cross-account access needed — delete the entire statement. • Specific external accounts — "Principal": { "AWS": ["arn:aws:iam::<account-id-1>:root", "arn:aws:iam::<account-id- 2>:root"] } • All accounts within your AWS Organization — keep "Principal": "*" but add a Condition: "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:PrincipalOrgID": "<o-xxxxxxxxxx>" } } 2. Apply the corrected policy: aws ecr set-repository-policy --repository-name <repo-name> --region $AWS_REGION \ --policy-text file:///tmp/repo-policy.json • If the repository should have no policy at all, delete it instead: aws ecr delete-repository-policy --repository-name <repo-name> --region $AWS_REGION 3. For a Failed registry policy, apply the same logic via aws ecr put-registry- policy --policy-text file:///tmp/registry-policy.json or remove with aws ecr delete-registry-policy --region $AWS_REGION.
attributes.AuditProcedure: 1. List all private ECR repositories in the region: aws ecr describe-repositories --region $AWS_REGION \ --query 'repositories[].repositoryName' --output table 2. For each repository returned above, retrieve its repository policy (if any) and inspect the principal and conditions on each statement: aws ecr get-repository-policy --repository-name <repo-name> --region $AWS_REGION \ --query 'policyText' --output text • A repository with no policy returns RepositoryPolicyNotFoundException — this is a Pass (default-deny applies). • The repository Fails if its policy contains any statement where all of the following are true: o Effect is Allow o Action includes any of 'ecr:*', 'ecr:BatchGetImage', 'ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer', 'ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability', 'ecr:DescribeImages', 'ecr:GetAuthorizationToken', 'ecr:PutImage', 'ecr:InitiateLayerUpload', 'ecr:UploadLayerPart', 'ecr:CompleteLayerUpload', or any wildcard expansion thereof o Principal is * or "AWS": "*" o Condition is absent OR does not restrict access to specific accounts/organizations (e.g., no 'aws:PrincipalAccount', 'aws:PrincipalOrgID', 'aws:SourceVpce', or equivalent constraint) 3. Also check the registry-wide policy, which applies to all repositories in the account: aws ecr get-registry-policy --region $AWS_REGION --query 'policyText' -- output text • Apply the same evaluation criteria to registry-policy statements. A RegistryPolicyNotFoundException response is a Pass.
